The three main causes for the financial challenges facing the universities were the impact of the demographic dip of 18-year-olds, which was deeper and longer in Wales than it was elsewhere in the UK. There were increased pension costs and, actually, increased costs generally. And, of course, there was current uncertainty as a result of the Augar review in England, and whether that might play into Wales, and also Brexit.

The meeting discussed that Cardiff University had had a bond rather than borrowing, which they drew down as they were spending. In the short term, the reserves of Cardiff would appear as though they have significant cash balances, but all of those were restricted for investment in the estate and, over the next two or three years, would be utilised for that.

The government had a quality machinery that they operated where they would expect institutions to be able to demonstrate that they've put in place appropriate arrangements to ensure that students can finish their programmes of study. They were not going to be recruiting students to programmes that they were not planning to continue—they just were not going to do that. In a market context, it would be suicidal for a university to treat their students like that.

The government had a machinery with 70/80 different factors and hundreds of questions that they asked twice a year to interrogate the performance of the institutions and to make sure that they were seeing them managing the issues that they were facing. The government had proper governance oversight. In all of those instances, there was staff and student engagement as well in the strategic approach on estates. The government had two bits to this. One was that the governance machinery within the institutions was structured appropriately to look at that. The other was that if the institutions were wanting to engage in anything other than relatively trivial borrowing, they had to get the government's consent as well.

Dr David Blaney said that there was no evidence that any governing bodies were exhibiting what might be considered to be an imprudent risk appetite. He explained that they would see this coming through in forecasts and requests for borrowings, predominantly. He also said that they had links into institutions that were informal and they had formal stuff. The machinery depended on having a body like HEFCW doing some of that role, and the people who lend money to institutions were absolutely clear about that.

The meeting discussed the need to include more people in risk management. The team had a slightly different perspective and had a perspective that was very intimately informed in terms of how the institution was performing. They had a governing body with a range of perspectives and had people who were very committed and very enthusiastic about the institution. They had conversations with both governing bodies and executives.

The direction of travel was that the sector in Wales was seeing an increased risk profile, and it was about the financial pressures that had already been discussed this morning. The efforts that the Minister had gone to to secure the Diamond settlement, and, indeed, other bits of money now and again, were so important. The institutions had been working very hard to try not to take cost out now that they really didn't have to take out, because they didn't want to reduce capacity, which they would struggle to recover again when the financial position improved. So, they were seeing deficits, which were managed deficits, where they were spending more than their income in order just to keep the capacity in.

The discourse status is the active or inaccessible status of the discourse.
